newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine PM's removal seen affecting gas trade.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine PM's removal seen affecting gas trade.

text.p: Removal of Ukraine's Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko from his position is likely to have an impact on the gas market, where Ukraine has made its biggest money in the last couple years, analysts and gas traders said on Friday.

President Leonid Kuchma issued a decree on Thursday citing illness as the reason for removing Lazarenko from the post he had occupied for a year, and appointed First Deputy Prime Minister Vasyl Durdynets as acting premier.

"There will definitely be an impact on the (gas trading) scheme, but probably not immediately. The speed of the impact will depend on who replaces Lazarenko," Vyacheslav Pikhovshek, head of the Independent Political Research Centre, told Reuters.
Local media have said Lazarenko will not return to the job as Ukraine's fifth premier in as many years of independence.

Lazarenko was behind a scheme introduced in 1995 which transferred distribution of imported Russian gas from state hands to several private traders. Lazarenko defended the scheme, which he said helped slash energy debts to Russia.
But critics said traders did not pay all their taxes, leaving Ukraine short of money to pay off a growing wage backlog of nearly $2.2 billion in unpaid wages.
Recently Kuchma and his top aides criticised it for creating a monopolistic, uncompetitive energy market.

The New York Times published an article recently quoting Western intelligence reports estimating Lazarenko had gained about $200 million from unofficial involvement in United Energy Systems of Ukraine (UESU), the biggest trader of Russian gas.
"Neither Pavlo Lazarenko, nor his children, nor relatives have any links or shares in United Energy Systems," the corporation's spokesman, Petro Yakovchuk, told Reuters.
President Yulia Tymoshenko, whose company has an annual turnover of $10 billion, has said the company was not enjoying protection from the government and Lazarenko.

"All denials of links with the gas market by Lazarenko are doubtful. The UESU got its share not because of a tender but through a direct decision by the government," Pikhovshek said. "This was real protectionism by the head of the government."
Pikhovshek also mentioned that both Lazarenko and the UESU originated from the eastern industrial city of Dnipropetrovsk -- also hometown to Kuchma and other top government members.
One gas trader said it was unlikely Ukraine would go back to the days of the state-owned Ukrgazprom, but that it would alter shares in volumes and make the system more competitive.
"This scheme is quite stable. But the shares are likely to be re-divided again," the trader added.

"I think that regardless of the person (Lazarenko), Ukraine faces reforms in the energy sector," Valery Lytvytsky, Kuchma's top economic advisor, said on Friday, adding the president was firm on reducing Ukrainian gas consumption by 20 per cent.
"That cannot be achieved without modernisation of the gas-trading scheme and demonopolisation of the market. It will be done regardless of (Lazarenko's) illness," Lytvytsky added.
Ukraine is one of the biggest consumers of Russian gas -- with supplies from Russia's gas monopoly Gazprom forecast at 53 billion cubic metres this year.
Up to 20 bcm will be imported from the Central Asian states of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, adding to Ukraine's annual domestic output of 18 bcm.

The UESU is due to import and sell 15.5 bcm this year, with Intergaz company at 8.3 bcm and Ukrgazprom up to ten billion cubic metres. Itera Ukraine Corporation, which was due to import about 13 bcm of Turkmen gas, was removed from the Ukrainian market due to problems with payments to Turkmenistan.
